help.2048.end: You win at 2048, and may keep going. The game ends when no move is left.
help.2048.goal: Make a tile with the number 2048.
help.2048.keys: Arrow keys or W, A, S and D slide every tile. Z undoes one move. On a phone, swipe on the board.
help.2048.tip: Keep your biggest tile in a corner.
help.2048.turn: Slide all tiles one way. Two equal tiles that meet join into one with their sum.
help.babel.end: Each game is five words. The fewer clues you need, the more you score.
help.babel.goal: Name the English word from its translations.
help.babel.keys: Type the word and press Enter.
help.babel.tip: Words that look alike in several languages often share a root.
help.babel.turn: You see two clues in other languages. Type the English word. A wrong guess, or Another clue, shows one more.
help.backgammon.end: The first to bear all checkers off wins.
help.backgammon.goal: Move all 15 of your checkers home and off the board first.
help.backgammon.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes the last step, N starts a new game.
help.backgammon.tip: Two checkers together on a point are safe.
help.backgammon.turn: Roll the dice, then move checkers by each number. Landing on a lone checker sends it to the bar. You cannot land on a point with two or more.
help.belote.end: Play eight tricks. The team that bid must score more than half the points.
help.belote.goal: Win more points than the other team.
help.belote.tip: Holding king and queen of trump scores a bonus.
help.belote.turn: Choose trump, then play one card to each trick and follow suit. Trump cards are worth more.
help.bigtwo.end: The first player out wins the round.
help.bigtwo.goal: Be first to play all your cards.
help.bigtwo.turn: Play a higher card, pair, three or five-card hand of the same kind as the last one, or pass.
help.blackbox.end: Mark every ball, then tap the Check button that appears. You win if your balls give the same beam results.
help.blackbox.goal: Find the balls hidden in the box.
help.blackbox.tip: H means a beam hit a ball head-on. R means it came straight back.
help.blackbox.turn: Tap an edge square to fire a beam. Tap squares inside to mark balls. Beams bend around balls and stop if they hit one.
help.blackjack.end: The dealer plays after you. Closest to 21 wins.
help.blackjack.goal: Get closer to 21 than the dealer without going over.
help.blackjack.tip: Cards 2 to 10 count their number, picture cards count 10, ace is 1 or 11.
help.blackjack.turn: Hit to take a card, stand to stop. Double or split when it helps.
help.blast.end: The round ends when only one bomber is left.
help.blast.keys: Player 1: W, A, S and D, Space drops a bomb. Player 2: arrow keys and Enter. With one player the arrow keys also walk. P pauses. Swipe or use the arrows.
help.blast.tip: Never stand in line with your own bomb.
help.blast.turn: Walk the grid and drop bombs to break blocks and catch the others in the blast. Pick up power-ups for range, more bombs and speed.
help.bluff.end: You score 2 for the real meaning and 1 for each friend your fake fools.
help.bluff.goal: Fool your friends, and find the real meaning.
help.bluff.tip: Copy the style of a dictionary: short, plain and sure of itself.
help.bluff.turn: Each person writes a fake meaning for the word in private. Then each votes in private for the one they think is real.
help.bricks.end: You clear a level when no bricks are left. You lose when the ball is gone and no lives remain.
help.bricks.keys: Arrow keys or A and D move the paddle. Space launches. P pauses. On a phone, drag along the board and tap to launch.
help.bricks.tip: Hit the ball with the paddle’s edge to steer it.
help.bricks.turn: Move the paddle to bounce the ball. Where the ball lands on the paddle sets its angle.
help.bridge.end: After 13 tricks the score is added up. Making your bid scores; falling short costs.
help.bridge.goal: Win the number of tricks you bid, with your partner.
help.bridge.tip: Count your high card points before you bid.
help.bridge.turn: Bid in turn. Then play a card to each trick and follow the suit led. The player to the left of the declarer leads.
help.bridges.end: You win when every island has its number of bridges and all the islands are linked.
help.bridges.goal: Connect every island with bridges. Each number says how many bridges touch that island.
help.bridges.tip: Tap a finished island to lock it. Press and hold, then drag, to mark where no bridge goes.
help.bridges.turn: Drag from one island toward another to build a bridge. Drag again for a second one. Bridges never cross.
help.canasta.end: The hand ends when someone goes out, which takes two canastas. Cards left in your hand count against you.
help.canasta.goal: Be first to reach the goal score by melding cards, making canastas (seven of a rank) and going out.
help.canasta.keys: Keys: D draws, T takes the pile, M melds, X discards, Escape clears your picks.
help.canasta.tip: A wild card on the pile freezes it: only a natural pair from your hand matching the top card takes it.
help.canasta.turn: Draw two cards, or take the discard pile. Lay down three or more cards of one rank, then discard one. Twos and jokers are wild.
help.carrom.end: The round ends when one side has pocketed all their coins and covered the queen.
help.carrom.goal: Pocket all your coins, then the queen.
help.carrom.keys: Arrow keys place the striker, A and D aim, W and S set the power, Enter shoots.
help.carrom.tip: Pocket the queen, then one of your own coins to cover it.
help.carrom.turn: Place the striker on your line, aim and flick. Pocket your own coins and keep your turn.
help.checkers.end: You win when the other side cannot move.
help.checkers.goal: Capture all the other side’s pieces, or leave them with no move.
help.checkers.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, N starts a new game.
help.checkers.tip: A piece that reaches the far row becomes a king and moves both ways.
help.checkers.turn: Move a piece one square diagonally forward. Jump over a piece to capture it. You must capture if you can.
help.chess.end: Checkmate wins. Stalemate and repeated positions are draws.
help.chess.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, F flips the board, N starts a new game.
help.chess.tip: Control the centre and bring out your knights and bishops early.
help.chess.turn: Move one piece. Each kind of piece moves in its own way. If your king is attacked, you must protect it.
help.chessopenings.end: The line ends when its moves run out. Play something else and it tells you what the line plays.
help.chessopenings.goal: Learn a named opening by playing your side of it.
help.chessopenings.keys: Tap a piece, then a square. H shows a hint, R restarts the line, N is the next line.
help.chessopenings.tip: Choose an opening family, and Next line picks another line from it.
help.chessopenings.turn: Play the book move for your side. Zimi answers with the book move for the other side.
help.chesspuzzles.end: Solve it cleanly and your puzzle rating goes up. A miss or a hint counts against it.
help.chesspuzzles.goal: Find the best move, then keep finding it until the puzzle ends.
help.chesspuzzles.keys: Tap a piece, then a square. H shows a hint, N is the next puzzle.
help.chesspuzzles.tip: Hint first shows which piece to move, then where.
help.chesspuzzles.turn: Watch the opponent move, then tap a piece and a square. A wrong move lets you try again.
help.chinesecheckers.end: The first to fill the opposite corner wins.
help.chinesecheckers.goal: Move all ten of your marbles to the opposite corner.
help.chinesecheckers.keys: Arrow keys move the cursor, Enter selects, U undoes, N starts a new game.
help.chinesecheckers.tip: Build a ladder of marbles to hop a long way.
help.chinesecheckers.turn: Move one marble to an adjacent hole, or hop over marbles in a chain.
help.circuit.end: The race ends after the last lap. Your best lap is kept as a ghost to race next time.
help.circuit.goal: Finish first, or set your best lap.
help.circuit.keys: Arrows or WASD steer, accelerate and brake. R puts the car back on track, P pauses. Two players: WASD and the arrows.
help.circuit.tip: Brake before the corner, not in it.
help.circuit.turn: Steer with the arrow keys or the touch zones. Ease off in tight corners. Hard turns make the car slide.
help.codebreaker.end: You win when you crack it, or lose when your guesses run out.
help.codebreaker.goal: Crack the secret code of 4 pegs.
help.codebreaker.keys: Keys 1 to 6 place a peg, Backspace erases one, Enter checks.
help.codebreaker.tip: Use each answer to rule things out.
help.codebreaker.turn: Make a guess. A solid dot means a right peg in the right place. A ring means a right peg in the wrong place.
help.crazyeights.end: The first player with no cards wins the round.
help.crazyeights.goal: Be first to play all your cards.
help.crazyeights.tip: Keep an eight for when you are stuck.
help.crazyeights.turn: Play a card that matches the top card by suit or by rank. If you cannot, draw. An eight can be played at any time. Then you name the suit.
help.cribbage.end: The first player to reach 121 wins.
help.cribbage.tip: Count the hand carefully; fifteens and pairs add up quickly.
help.cribbage.turn: Give two cards to the crib. Then take turns playing cards, keeping the running count at 31 or under. Score for pairs, runs and fifteens.
help.crossing.end: Fill all five nests to clear the level. Each level is faster.
help.crossing.goal: Get your chick across the road and the river to a nest.
help.crossing.keys: Arrow keys or W, A, S and D hop one tile. P pauses. Swipe or use the arrows.
help.crossing.tip: Wait for a gap rather than rushing.
help.crossing.turn: Hop one step at a time. Dodge the cars, and ride the logs and turtles across the water.
help.cube.end: You win when every face of the cube is blue.
help.cube.goal: Roll the cube until all six blue squares are on its six faces.
help.cube.tip: Look ahead before each roll. Try to finish in fewer moves each time.
help.cube.turn: Tap a square next to the cube, or use the arrow keys, to roll it there. Touching faces swap colors.
help.dominoes.end: The round ends when someone plays their last domino or nobody can move.
help.dominoes.goal: Get rid of all your dominoes first.
help.dominoes.keys: Tab to a tile, Enter plays it, N starts a new game.
help.dominoes.tip: Count the dots left in the other hands to see who is ahead.
help.dominoes.turn: Play a domino that matches an open end of the line. If you cannot, draw from the boneyard, or pass in the Block game.
help.dominosa.end: You win when every square is covered and no pair of numbers repeats.
help.dominosa.goal: Cover the grid with dominoes. Each pair of numbers must appear exactly once.
help.dominosa.tip: Start with a pair that can fit in only one place.
help.dominosa.turn: Tap the gap between two numbers to place a domino there. Press and hold to mark two numbers as not paired.
help.dotsandboxes.end: When every line is drawn, the most boxes wins.
help.dotsandboxes.goal: Close more boxes than the other side.
help.dotsandboxes.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter draws, U undoes, H gives a hint, N starts a new game.
help.dotsandboxes.tip: Avoid drawing the third side of a box.
help.dotsandboxes.turn: Draw one line between two dots. Closing a box scores it, and you move again.
help.draughts.end: You win when the other side cannot move.
help.draughts.goal: Capture all the other side’s pieces, or leave them with no move.
help.draughts.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, H hints, F flips, N starts a new game.
help.draughts.tip: Kings fly any distance along a diagonal.
help.draughts.turn: Move a piece one square diagonally forward. You must capture, and take the most pieces you can. Men may capture backwards.
help.droppin.end: Five places. Closer pins score more, up to 100 each.
help.droppin.goal: Put the pin as close to the place as you can.
help.droppin.tip: Find a big landmark nearby first, then zoom in.
help.droppin.turn: On your map, pan until the cross is on the place, then Drop pin. On the world, tap where it is, then Drop pin.
help.durak.end: The last player with cards is the durak, the fool.
help.durak.goal: Do not be the last player with cards.
help.durak.tip: If you cannot beat the cards, you pick them all up.
help.durak.turn: The attacker plays a card. The defender must beat it with a higher card of the same suit, or any trump. Others may add cards of the same rank.
help.echo.end: The game ends at your first mistake.
help.echo.goal: Repeat the sequence for as long as you can.
help.echo.keys: Press 1 to 4, or Q, W, A and S for the four corners. Space or P pauses.
help.echo.tip: Say the colours out loud as you watch.
help.echo.turn: Watch the pads light up, then tap them in the same order. The sequence gets one longer each round.
help.euchre.end: The game ends when a team reaches 10.
help.euchre.goal: Be the first team to 10 points by winning tricks.
help.euchre.tip: Going alone scores more, and risks more.
help.euchre.turn: Decide whether to name trump. Then play one card per trick and follow the suit led. The jack of trump is the highest card.
help.fifteen.end: You win when the numbers run in order from the top left.
help.fifteen.goal: Slide the tiles into number order, with the gap at the bottom right.
help.fifteen.tip: Solve the top row first, then the next one, and leave the last two rows for the end.
help.fifteen.turn: Tap a tile next to the gap to slide it in. Tap farther along the row to slide several tiles at once.
help.filling.end: You win when every group matches its number.
help.filling.goal: Fill in numbers so each connected group of one number has exactly that many squares.
help.filling.tip: A 1 never touches another 1. Start there.
help.filling.turn: Tap a square, then tap a digit. Drag across squares to fill several at once.
help.firstlines.end: The round ends after the last line, and your score shows.
help.firstlines.goal: Name the book from its opening line.
help.firstlines.keys: Press 1 to 4 to answer. Enter goes on.
help.firstlines.tip: The author shows once you answer.
help.firstlines.turn: Read the line, then tap the title you think it opens.
help.fiveletters.end: You win when you guess it, or lose after six tries.
help.fiveletters.goal: Find the hidden five-letter word in six tries.
help.fiveletters.keys: Type letters, then press Enter. Backspace deletes.
help.fiveletters.tip: Start with a word that has common letters. The daily word is the same for everyone today.
help.fiveletters.turn: Type a word and enter it. Green means right letter, right place. Amber means right letter, wrong place. Gray means the letter is not in the word.
help.flags.end: The round ends after the last flag, and your score shows.
help.flags.goal: Name the country from its flag.
help.flags.keys: Press 1 to 4 to answer. Enter goes on.
help.flags.tip: Look at the colors first, then the shapes.
help.flags.turn: Look at the flag, then tap the country it belongs to.
help.fleet.end: You win when every enemy ship is sunk.
help.fleet.goal: Sink all Zimi’s ships before it sinks yours.
help.fleet.keys: Arrow keys move between squares, R turns a ship.
help.fleet.tip: After a hit, try the squares next to it.
help.fleet.turn: Place your ships. Then tap a square in the enemy sea to fire. Hits are marked.
help.flip.end: You win when all the squares are lit.
help.flip.tip: Flipping a square twice cancels out, so the order of your moves does not matter.
help.flip.turn: Tap a square to flip it and the squares shown in its small diagram. Light squares turn dark and dark ones turn light.
help.flood.end: You win when the grid is one color within the limit. You lose when the moves run out.
help.flood.goal: Fill the whole grid with one color within the move limit.
help.flood.tip: Pick colors that touch the most new squares, and work outward from the corner.
help.flood.turn: Tap any square. The top-left block, and everything joined to it, turns that square’s color.
help.fourinarow.end: Four in a row, across, up or diagonal, wins. A full board is a draw.
help.fourinarow.goal: Be first to line up four discs.
help.fourinarow.keys: Arrow keys choose a column, Enter drops, U undoes, H gives a hint, N starts a new game.
help.fourinarow.tip: Watch for two threats at once.
help.fourinarow.turn: Drop a disc into a column. It falls to the lowest empty spot.
help.freecell.end: You win when every card is on the top piles.
help.freecell.goal: Move all 52 cards to the four piles at the top, each suit from ace up to king.
help.freecell.tip: Every deal is numbered, so you can play the same deal again.
help.freecell.turn: Build down on the table in alternating colours. Park a card in one of the four free cells when you need to.
help.galaxies.end: You win when every region is closed, balanced around its dot, and has no extra lines inside.
help.galaxies.goal: Split the grid into regions. Each must look the same turned upside down, with one dot at its center.
help.galaxies.tip: A square and its mirror image through the dot always belong to the same region.
help.galaxies.turn: Tap a grid line to draw or erase a border. Press and hold a dot, then drag, to leave a reminder arrow.
help.gin.end: The hand ends when someone knocks. Play until a player reaches 100.
help.gin.goal: Make sets and runs, and keep the leftover cards worth as little as you can.
help.gin.tip: Using all ten cards in sets and runs is gin, and earns a bonus.
help.gin.turn: Draw a card, then discard one. When your leftover cards total 10 or less, you may knock.
help.go.end: When both pass, mark dead stones. Your score is your territory plus captured stones. White gets 6.5 extra points.
help.go.goal: Surround more of the board than the other side.
help.go.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter places, U undoes, H gives a hint, N starts a new game.
help.go.tip: Stones in a connected group live or die together.
help.go.turn: Place one stone on a crossing, or pass. Stones with no free neighbour are captured.
help.golf.end: You win when the columns are empty.
help.golf.goal: Move every card from the columns to the pile.
help.golf.tip: Ace and king do not wrap around.
help.golf.turn: Tap a column card that is one higher or one lower than the pile card. Tap the deck when stuck.
help.gomoku.end: Five in a row, in any direction, wins.
help.gomoku.goal: Get five stones in a row.
help.gomoku.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter places, U undoes, H gives a hint, N starts a new game.
help.gomoku.tip: An open row of four cannot be stopped.
help.gomoku.turn: Place one stone on any empty crossing.
help.goproblems.end: The problem is solved when the group is settled: captured, unable to make two eyes, or alive.
help.goproblems.goal: Kill the marked white group, or make the marked black group live.
help.goproblems.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter plays. U undoes, H shows the key point, R restarts, N is the next problem.
help.goproblems.tip: Look for the vital point: the one spot both sides want.
help.goproblems.turn: You play Black. Tap a point. If it works, White answers with its most stubborn move.
help.group.end: You win when the grid is full and follows every rule.
help.group.goal: Complete the grid so each letter appears once in every row and column, and the pattern stays consistent.
help.group.tip: Fill squares that have only one possible letter first.
help.group.turn: Tap a square, then tap a letter or press its key. Press and hold to write small notes.
help.guess.end: You win when a guess matches the hidden row. You lose when you run out of guesses.
help.guess.goal: Work out the hidden row of colored pegs within the allowed number of guesses.
help.guess.tip: A white mark means a right color in the wrong place. Use each guess to rule colors out.
help.guess.turn: Drag colored pegs into the current row, then confirm the guess. A black mark means the right color in the right place.
help.hearts.end: The game ends when someone reaches 100. Lowest score wins.
help.hearts.goal: Finish with the fewest points. Each heart is 1 point, the queen of spades is 13.
help.hearts.tip: Take all the hearts and the queen of spades to shoot the moon: you score 0 and the others get 26.
help.hearts.turn: Pass three cards first. Then play one card per trick. Follow the suit led if you can. The highest card of that suit wins the trick.
help.hex.end: The first chain across wins. There are no draws.
help.hex.goal: Link your two sides of the board with an unbroken chain of your stones.
help.hex.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter places, U undoes, H gives a hint, N starts a new game.
help.hex.tip: The centre is strong. With the swap rule on, the second player may take over the first move.
help.hex.turn: Place one stone on any empty hexagon.
help.higherlower.end: The round ends after the last pair, and your score shows.
help.higherlower.goal: Say which of two things is greater.
help.higherlower.keys: Press 1 or 2 to answer. Enter goes on.
help.higherlower.tip: The answer shows the real figures, so you learn as you go.
help.higherlower.turn: Read the question, then tap the one with more people, a larger area, a taller peak or a longer course.
help.hnefatafl.end: The king reaching a corner wins for the defenders. Capturing the king wins for the attackers.
help.hnefatafl.goal: Attackers: capture the king. Defenders: get the king to a corner.
help.hnefatafl.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, H hints, N starts a new game.
help.hnefatafl.tip: The king is captured by four attackers, or three and the throne.
help.hnefatafl.turn: Move a piece in a straight line any distance. Trap a piece between two of yours to capture it.
help.holdem.end: At the showdown the best hand wins the pot.
help.holdem.goal: Win chips by making the best five-card hand, or by making others fold.
help.holdem.tip: Fold weak hands and bet strong ones.
help.holdem.turn: You get two private cards, and five shared cards are dealt. Bet, call, raise or fold in each round.
help.hopper.end: Touch the flag to finish the level. Lose all your hearts and the game is over.
help.hopper.goal: Reach the flag at the end of each level.
help.hopper.keys: Arrow keys or A and D run. Space, Up or W jumps; hold to jump higher. P pauses.
help.hopper.tip: You can still jump a moment after leaving a ledge.
help.hopper.turn: Run left and right and jump. Hold jump longer to jump higher. Collect coins and avoid the creatures.
help.inertia.end: You win when the last gem is collected. Hitting a mine ends the game.
help.inertia.goal: Collect every gem without touching a mine.
help.inertia.tip: Plan around the stop squares: the ball can only change direction where it stops.
help.inertia.turn: Tap a direction from the ball. It slides until a wall or a stop square halts it, picking up gems on the way.
help.janggi.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, P passes, H hints, F flips, N starts a new game.
help.janggi.tip: Bikjang: when the generals face each other, the side to move must break it or pass, and a pass is a draw.
help.janggi.turn: Move one piece. Cannons jump over exactly one piece. The general stays in the palace.
help.jigsaw.end: You finish when the picture is whole.
help.jigsaw.tip: Start with the edges. Hold Peek to see the whole picture.
help.jigsaw.turn: Drag a piece to where it belongs. Pieces that fit click together.
help.kart.end: A race is three laps. A Grand Prix adds up the points from a cup of races.
help.kart.goal: Finish ahead of the other seven racers.
help.kart.keys: Arrows or W, A, S and D drive. Hold Shift in a bend to drift, let go for a boost. Space uses the item. P pauses. Two players: W, A, S and D with Left Shift and Space, and the arrows with Right Shift and Enter.
help.kart.tip: Hold a drift through the whole corner, then let go for the boost.
help.kart.turn: Drive, drift through corners to charge a boost, and grab the orange cubes for an item: Boost, Slick, Spark, Shield or Magnet.
help.keen.end: You win when the grid is full and every group is correct.
help.keen.goal: Fill the grid with digits so none repeats in a row or column. Each outlined group must make its number with the sign shown.
help.keen.tip: Start with groups of one square, and with products that only certain digits can make.
help.keen.turn: Tap a square, then tap a digit. Press and hold a square to write small notes instead.
help.koikoi.end: When you form a yaku, you may stop and score, or call koi-koi to keep going for more.
help.koikoi.goal: Score the most points over the months.
help.koikoi.tip: Calling koi-koi is a gamble: the other side can score too.
help.koikoi.turn: Match a card from your hand to a card on the table by flower. Then turn the top of the deck. Form yaku, the scoring sets, to win a round.
help.lander.end: A gentle, upright landing on the pad wins. Anything else crashes.
help.lander.goal: Land softly on the pad before the fuel runs out.
help.lander.keys: Arrow keys or A and D rotate, Up, W or Space thrusts, P pauses. Land with Down under 35 and Side under 22.
help.lander.tip: Cut the thrust to save fuel, and slow down early.
help.lander.turn: Rotate to aim and thrust to slow down. Gravity pulls you the whole time.
help.lastline.end: You lose if the drones reach the bottom or your lives run out. Clear all drones to move on.
help.lastline.goal: Stop the drones before they reach your line.
help.lastline.keys: Arrow keys or A and D move, Space fires, P pauses.
help.lastline.tip: Shoot the outer drones first to slow the march.
help.lastline.turn: Move along the bottom and shoot upward. Shields wear away when hit.
help.letterbyletter.end: You win when the word is complete.
help.letterbyletter.goal: Guess the word before the balloon goes down.
help.letterbyletter.keys: Type a letter on your keyboard to pick it.
help.letterbyletter.tip: Start with vowels and common letters. The daily word is the same for everyone today.
help.letterbyletter.turn: Pick a letter. A right letter fills in. A wrong one costs the balloon some air.
help.liarsdice.end: A wrong bidder or wrong caller loses a die. The last player with a die wins.
help.liarsdice.goal: Be the last player with dice.
help.liarsdice.keys: ↑ and ↓ change the count, 1 to 6 pick the number, ↵ bids, L calls Liar.
help.liarsdice.tip: Count your own dice first. They are part of the total.
help.liarsdice.turn: Look at your dice. Bid how many dice of a number are under all the cups, higher than the last bid, or call the last bid a lie. Ones are wild, unless ones are the number bid.
help.lightup.end: You win when every square is lit and each number touches exactly that many lamps.
help.lightup.goal: Light every square by placing lamps. No lamp may light another.
help.lightup.tip: A black square with a 0 has no lamp beside it. Start there.
help.lightup.turn: Tap a square to place a lamp. Press and hold to mark a square that cannot hold one.
help.loopy.end: You win when the loop closes, never crosses itself, and satisfies every number.
help.loopy.goal: Draw one single loop. Each number says how many sides of its square the loop uses.
help.loopy.tip: Begin with a 0, and with a 3 beside another 3.
help.loopy.turn: Tap a line to draw it. Tap again to erase it. Press and hold to mark a line as unused.
help.ludo.end: The first player with all four pieces home wins.
help.ludo.goal: Bring all four of your pieces home.
help.ludo.keys: Tab picks a token, Enter moves it, R rolls, 1 to 4 pick a token, N starts a new game.
help.ludo.tip: A six also gives you another roll.
help.ludo.turn: Roll the die. A six lets a piece out of the yard. Move a piece that many steps round the cross. Land on a lone rival to send it home.
help.magnets.end: You win when every count matches and no two like poles touch.
help.magnets.goal: Fill the board with magnets and blank tiles so the numbers at the edges count the poles in each row and column.
help.magnets.tip: Like poles repel, so they may not sit side by side. Use that to rule out placements.
help.magnets.turn: Tap an empty tile to place a magnet. Tap again to turn it around. Press and hold to mark a tile as blank.
help.mahjong.end: You win when no tiles are left.
help.mahjong.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter picks, H hint, S shuffle, U undo.
help.mahjong.tip: Free the tiles that block the most others first.
help.mahjong.turn: Tap two matching free tiles. A tile is free when nothing is on top and its left or right side is open.
help.mahjong4.end: The round ends when someone wins or the wall runs out. Points follow the scoring table.
help.mahjong4.goal: Be first to complete a hand: four sets and a pair.
help.mahjong4.keys: Arrow keys move over your tiles, Enter picks and discards, H hints, N starts a new game.
help.mahjong4.tip: Keep your options open early. Do not hold too many single tiles.
help.mahjong4.turn: Draw a tile, then discard one. You may take another player’s discard to finish a set. Call win when your hand is complete.
help.makruk.end: You win by checkmate. A count may end a drawn game.
help.makruk.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, H hints, F flips, N starts a new game.
help.makruk.tip: Keep your pieces together. The queen is weak.
help.makruk.turn: Move one piece. The pieces are like chess but weaker. Pawns promote on the sixth row.
help.mancala.end: The game ends when seeds run out. The larger store wins.
help.mancala.goal: Capture more seeds than the other side.
help.mancala.keys: Tap one of your pits, or use the arrow keys and Enter. U undoes, H gives a hint, N starts a new game.
help.mancala.tip: Plan so that your last seed lands where it captures.
help.mancala.turn: Pick up the seeds in one of your pits and sow them one by one round the board. The last seed can win seeds.
help.map.end: You win when every region is colored and no neighbors match.
help.map.goal: Color every region with one of four colors so no two neighbors share a color.
help.map.tip: Regions that touch only at a corner may share a color.
help.map.turn: Drag a color onto a region. Press and hold a region to mark colors it cannot be.
help.memory.end: You finish when every pair is found.
help.memory.keys: Tab or the arrow keys move between cards. Enter turns a card over.
help.memory.turn: Turn over two cards. If they match they stay up. If not they turn back.
help.mines.end: You win when every safe square is open. Opening a mine ends the game.
help.mines.goal: Open every square that has no mine.
help.mines.tip: The first tap is always safe, and you never need to guess.
help.mines.turn: Tap a square to open it. Press and hold to place a flag. A number counts the mines in the squares around it.
help.minesweeper.end: You win when only mines are left. Opening a mine ends the game.
help.minesweeper.goal: Open every square that has no mine.
help.minesweeper.keys: Arrows move, Space opens, F flags, C opens around a number. On a touch screen, press and hold to flag.
help.minesweeper.tip: Your first tap is always safe.
help.minesweeper.turn: Tap a square to open it. A number tells how many of the eight squares around it hold a mine. Flag the ones you know are mines.
help.minicrossword.end: You finish when every square is right.
help.minicrossword.goal: Fill the grid so every word across and down is right.
help.minicrossword.keys: Arrow keys move. Space switches direction.
help.minicrossword.tip: Hint reveals a letter. Check marks the wrong ones.
help.minicrossword.turn: Tap a square, read the clue above, and type. Tap the square again to switch between across and down.
help.morris.end: You win when the other side has two pieces or cannot move.
help.morris.goal: Reduce the other side to two pieces, or leave them with no move.
help.morris.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, H gives a hint, N starts a new game.
help.morris.tip: With only three pieces left, yours may fly to any point.
help.morris.turn: First place your pieces one by one. Then slide them along the lines. Three in a row is a mill: remove an opponent piece.
help.mosaic.end: You win when every number is correct.
help.mosaic.goal: Color squares so each number matches the count of colored squares in the 3 by 3 block around it.
help.mosaic.tip: A number counts its own square too. A 0 clears all nine squares, and a 9 colors all nine.
help.mosaic.turn: Tap a square to color it black. Press and hold to mark it white. Tap again to clear it.
help.muncher.end: Clear the maze to move on. Lose all your lives and the game ends.
help.muncher.goal: Eat every dot in the maze.
help.muncher.keys: Arrow keys or W, A, S and D steer. You keep moving until you turn. P pauses. Swipe or use the arrows.
help.muncher.tip: Each chaser has its own habit. Learn them.
help.muncher.turn: Steer through the maze with swipes or arrow keys. A power pellet turns the chasers blue for a while. Then you can eat them.
help.net.end: You win when every tile is joined to the center and no loop closes.
help.net.goal: Turn the tiles until they all link into one network with no closed loops.
help.net.tip: Work from the corners and edges, where tiles have fewer ways to turn.
help.net.turn: Tap a tile to turn it. Press and hold to turn it back. Two-finger tap locks it. Tiles joined to the center light up.
help.netslide.end: You win when every tile is joined to the center and no loop closes.
help.netslide.goal: Slide whole rows and columns until the tiles form one connected network with no closed loops.
help.netslide.tip: Settle the tiles near the center first, then link the rest to them.
help.netslide.turn: Tap an arrow at the edge of the grid to shift that row or column one step. Tiles that slide off wrap around.
help.noughts.end: Three in a row wins. A full board is a draw.
help.noughts.goal: Get three of your marks in a row.
help.noughts.keys: Tap a square, or move with the arrow keys and press Enter. X goes first.
help.noughts.tip: Take the centre, then a corner.
help.paddles.end: The first to the target score wins.
help.paddles.goal: Score points by getting the ball past the other paddle.
help.paddles.keys: Drag along your half of the court, or use the arrow keys. Two players: the top player uses A and D.
help.paddles.tip: Hit the ball with the paddle’s edge for a sharper angle.
help.paddles.turn: Slide your paddle along your end of the court to hit the ball back.
help.palisade.end: You win when every region has the right size and every number is satisfied.
help.palisade.goal: Divide the grid into regions of the same size. Each number says how many sides of its square are borders.
help.palisade.tip: The outer edge of the grid counts as a border.
help.palisade.turn: Tap a line between squares to place a border. Press and hold to mark a line as no border.
help.pattern.end: You win when every row and column matches its clue.
help.pattern.goal: Color the grid so the clues beside each row and column match the lengths of its colored runs.
help.pattern.tip: Begin with lines whose clues nearly fill the row. Some squares are certain.
help.pattern.turn: Tap a square to color it black. Press and hold to mark it white. Drag to fill several at once.
help.pearl.end: You win when the loop is closed and every circle is satisfied.
help.pearl.goal: Draw one closed loop through the pearls. Black and white circles tell you how the loop passes them.
help.pearl.tip: Black circles are corners with straight neighbors. White circles are straight, with at least one corner next to them.
help.pearl.turn: Drag between neighboring squares to draw loop segments. Press and hold, then drag, to mark where no line goes.
help.pegs.end: You win when one peg remains.
help.pegs.goal: Jump pegs over pegs to remove them until only one is left.
help.pegs.tip: Keep pegs close together. A lone peg cannot jump.
help.pegs.turn: Drag a peg over a neighboring peg into the empty hole behind it. The jumped peg is removed.
help.pet.end: There is no end. A neglected pet gets sad, and recovers with care.
help.pet.tip: A little care every day is better than a lot once a week. Nothing ever dies. Your pets are saved in this browser.
help.pet.turn: Feed it, play with it, keep it clean and let it sleep. It grows up over real days, even while the page is closed.
help.pinball.end: The game ends when the last ball drains.
help.pinball.goal: Score as many points as you can.
help.pinball.keys: Z or the left arrow works the left flipper, / or the right arrow the right one. Hold Space and let go to launch. On a phone, touch either half of the table and hold the lane to launch.
help.pinball.tip: Light all the lanes for a bonus.
help.pinball.turn: Pull the plunger to launch the ball. Use the flippers to keep it in play and hit the bumpers and lanes.
help.pyramid.end: You win when the pyramid is gone.
help.pyramid.goal: Clear the pyramid by removing pairs of cards that add up to 13.
help.pyramid.tip: Turn over the deck only when you have to.
help.pyramid.turn: Tap two free cards that add up to 13. A king is 13 alone. A card is free when nothing covers it.
help.quest.end: Win by defeating the Warden. Your progress is saved on this device.
help.quest.goal: Find your way through the land and defeat the Warden.
help.quest.keys: Arrow keys or W, A, S and D walk. Space, Enter or Z is the action: swing the sword, open a chest, read a sign. P pauses. Your place is saved in this browser. Swipe or use the arrows.
help.quest.tip: Beaten enemies sometimes drop a heart. If you are knocked out, you wake at the start and keep what you found.
help.quest.turn: Explore screen by screen, use your sword, find keys and open doors.
help.quizzical.end: The round ends after the last question, and your score shows.
help.quizzical.goal: Answer as many questions as you can.
help.quizzical.keys: Press 1 to 4 to answer. Enter goes on.
help.quizzical.tip: The questions come from the articles in your Wikipedia.
help.quizzical.turn: Read the question and tap an answer.
help.range.end: You win when every number is correct, no shaded squares touch, and the white squares form one area.
help.range.goal: Shade squares so each number counts the white squares it can see. White squares must stay connected.
help.range.tip: A number counts its own square, and numbered squares are never shaded.
help.range.turn: Tap a square to shade it. Press and hold to mark it as white.
help.rect.end: You win when every square belongs to one rectangle with the right area.
help.rect.goal: Divide the grid into rectangles. Each holds one number, equal to its area.
help.rect.tip: Large numbers in a corner or against an edge have fewer shapes to choose from.
help.rect.turn: Tap a grid line to draw or erase an edge. Drag across squares to draw a whole rectangle.
help.reversi.end: The game ends when neither side can move. More discs wins.
help.reversi.goal: Have more discs of your colour when the board is full.
help.reversi.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter places, U undoes, N starts a new game.
help.reversi.tip: Corners cannot be flipped. Try to take them.
help.reversi.turn: Place a disc so it traps a line of the other colour between two of yours. The trapped discs flip.
help.roadrush.end: Reach the last checkpoint to finish the stage. If the clock hits zero, the run ends.
help.roadrush.goal: Reach each checkpoint before the clock runs out.
help.roadrush.keys: Left and right arrows or A and D steer, Up or W accelerates, Down or S brakes, P pauses. On a phone, hold a side of the road to steer and both sides to brake.
help.roadrush.tip: Stay off the shoulder: the grass slows you down.
help.roadrush.turn: Steer through the bends and around traffic. Hills hide what is coming.
help.rocks.end: You lose a ship when you hit a rock or a saucer shot. The game ends when no ships are left.
help.rocks.goal: Destroy all the rocks and stay alive.
help.rocks.keys: Arrow keys or A and D turn, Up or W thrusts, Space fires, P pauses.
help.rocks.tip: Keep moving; a still ship is easy to hit.
help.rocks.turn: Turn, thrust and shoot. Big rocks split into smaller ones.
help.samegame.end: You win when the grid is clear. You lose when no group of two or more is left.
help.samegame.goal: Clear the grid by removing groups of same-colored blocks.
help.samegame.tip: Build one big group of a color before you remove it.
help.samegame.turn: Tap a group to select it. Tap it again to remove it. Larger groups score more.
help.scopa.end: When the cards run out, you score for most cards, the seven of coins, most coins and most sevens.
help.scopa.tip: Sweeping the table scores a point.
help.scopa.turn: Play a card from your hand. It captures a table card of the same value, or cards that add up to it. Clearing the table is a scopa.
help.shogi.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, F flips the board, N starts a new game.
help.shogi.tip: Captured pieces become yours. Drops are your strongest tool.
help.shogi.turn: Move one piece, or drop a piece you captured onto any empty square. Pieces that reach the far three rows may promote.
help.signpost.end: You win when the numbers form one unbroken chain from 1 to the last.
help.signpost.goal: Link the squares into one chain, numbered from 1 to the last, following each arrow’s direction.
help.signpost.tip: A link can reach any distance along the arrow. Start from the numbers shown.
help.signpost.turn: Drag from a square to another square its arrow points toward to link them. Press and hold a square to break its link.
help.singles.end: You win when no number repeats, no shaded squares touch, and the white squares form one area.
help.singles.goal: Shade squares so no number repeats in any row or column. Shaded squares may not touch, and white squares must stay connected.
help.singles.tip: When a number appears twice in a row or column, one of the two must be shaded.
help.singles.turn: Tap a square to shade it. Press and hold to circle it as definitely white.
help.sixteen.end: You win when all the numbers are in order.
help.sixteen.goal: Slide rows and columns until the numbers run in order from the top left.
help.sixteen.tip: Place tiles one at a time, and avoid disturbing the ones already in place.
help.sixteen.turn: Tap an arrow at the edge to slide that row or column one step. The tile that slides off appears at the other end.
help.skat.end: The player must reach 61 card points, or the bid fails.
help.skat.tip: Count your jacks before you bid.
help.skat.turn: Bid. The winner takes the two skat cards, discards two, and names the game. Then everyone plays tricks.
help.skydetective.end: Six questions, then your score. The sky is the real one for your place and time.
help.skydetective.goal: Name what you see in the sky tonight.
help.skydetective.keys: Press 1 to 4 to answer. For Find, use the arrow keys and Enter on the sky.
help.skydetective.tip: The Moon is the biggest light. Planets shine steadily and stars twinkle.
help.skydetective.turn: A ring asks what an object is. Find asks you to tap a named planet or star.
help.slant.end: You win when every square has a line, no loop closes, and every number is met.
help.slant.goal: Draw a diagonal line in every square so that no loops form and each circled number matches the lines touching it.
help.slant.tip: A 4 sits in the middle of four lines. A 0 has none touching it.
help.slant.turn: Tap a square to draw a backslash. Press and hold for a slash. Tap again to switch or clear.
help.snake.end: The game ends when the snake hits a wall (in the walled game) or itself.
help.snake.goal: Eat as much as you can without hitting anything.
help.snake.keys: Arrow keys or W, A, S and D steer. Space or P pauses. Swipe or use the arrows.
help.snake.tip: Make room before you grow long.
help.snake.turn: Steer with the arrow keys or swipe. The snake grows each time it eats.
help.snakesandladders.end: The first to land exactly on the last square wins.
help.snakesandladders.goal: Be first to reach the last square.
help.snakesandladders.keys: Tap the die, or press R or Space, to roll.
help.snakesandladders.turn: Roll the die and move that many squares. A ladder takes you up. A snake takes you down.
help.sokoban.end: The level is done when every crate sits on a ring.
help.sokoban.goal: Push every crate onto a ring.
help.sokoban.keys: Swipe on the board, use the pad, or the arrow keys. Z undoes. Restart is in the Menu. Levels: DeepMind Boxoban (Apache-2.0).
help.sokoban.tip: Never push a crate into a corner unless a ring is there. Undo is free.
help.sokoban.turn: Walk with a swipe, the arrows or the arrow keys. Walk into a crate to push it. You cannot pull.
help.solitaire.end: You win when every card is on the top piles.
help.solitaire.goal: Move all 52 cards to the four piles at the top, each suit from ace up to king.
help.solitaire.tip: Turn over the hidden cards first. Only a king can go in an empty column.
help.solitaire.turn: Build down on the table, alternating red and black. Tap the deck for more cards. Tap or drag a card to move it.
help.solo.end: You win when the grid is full and correct.
help.solo.goal: Fill the grid with digits so each row, column and block holds every digit once.
help.solo.tip: Look for a square where only one digit fits, or a digit with only one place left in a row.
help.solo.turn: Tap a square, then tap a digit. Press and hold a square to write small notes instead.
help.spades.end: Play until a team reaches the target score.
help.spades.goal: Win the tricks you bid, as a team of two.
help.spades.tip: Bid Nil to take no tricks for a big bonus. Too many extra tricks, called bags, cost points.
help.spades.turn: Bid how many tricks you expect. Then play one card per trick and follow the suit led. Spades beat every other suit.
help.spellingbee.end: Your rank rises with your points. A word that uses all seven letters is a pangram, worth a bonus.
help.spellingbee.goal: Make as many words as you can from seven letters.
help.spellingbee.keys: Type letters, Backspace to delete, Enter to try, Space to shuffle.
help.spellingbee.tip: Letters may repeat. Shuffle to see new shapes.
help.spellingbee.turn: Tap letters to spell a word of four or more letters that uses the middle one. Tap Enter.
help.spider.end: A finished run leaves the table. You win when all eight are gone.
help.spider.goal: Make eight runs of one suit, from king down to ace.
help.spider.tip: Only a run of one suit moves as a group. Keep suits together.
help.spider.turn: Move a card or a run onto a card one higher, of any suit. Tap the deck for a new row of cards.
help.stacker.end: The game ends when the stack reaches the top.
help.stacker.goal: Clear lines by filling every square across a row.
help.stacker.keys: Arrows move. Up or X turns, Z turns back. Down drops softly, Space drops hard. C holds. P pauses. On a phone, drag to move, tap to turn, flick down to drop, swipe up to hold.
help.stacker.tip: Keep the surface flat and leave one tall gap for the long piece.
help.stacker.turn: Pieces fall one at a time. Move and turn each one to fit, then let it drop. You may hold one piece for later.
help.sudoku.end: You win when the grid is full and correct.
help.sudoku.goal: Fill the grid so every row, column and box has the digits 1 to 9 once.
help.sudoku.keys: Arrow keys move, digits fill, N toggles pencil marks (or hold Shift), Backspace clears, Z undoes, H gives a hint.
help.sudoku.tip: Look for a square where only one digit fits.
help.sudoku.turn: Pick a square, then a digit. Use notes for digits you are unsure of.
help.teenpatti.end: When two players are left, one can ask for a show and the best hand wins the pot.
help.teenpatti.goal: Have the best three-card hand, or make everyone else fold.
help.teenpatti.tip: Three of a kind beats a straight flush.
help.teenpatti.turn: Put in chips each round. Play blind or look at your cards. Bet, fold or ask for a show.
help.telephone.end: The roles swap each round. Together you score 3, 2 or 1 for each article found.
help.telephone.goal: Work together: find each article from a clue.
help.telephone.tip: Do not use the name. Describe what it is, or what it did.
help.telephone.turn: One of you writes a clue for the article shown. Pass the phone. The other searches and guesses, up to three times.
help.tents.end: You win when every tree has its own tent, no two tents touch, and the counts match.
help.tents.goal: Place a tent beside each tree. Numbers at the edges count the tents in each row and column.
help.tents.tip: Tents never touch, even at corners, so mark the squares around each tent as grass.
help.tents.turn: Tap a square to place a tent. Press and hold to mark it as grass, with no tent.
help.tienlen.goal: Be first to play all your cards.
help.tienlen.tip: Twos are the highest. Four pairs in a row can chop a two.
help.tienlen.turn: Play a higher card, pair, three or run of the same kind as the last play, or pass.
help.timeline.end: You play three rounds. Each event in the right place scores a point.
help.timeline.goal: Put five events in the order they happened.
help.timeline.keys: Press 1 to 5 to pick an event. Enter checks.
help.timeline.tip: Start with the one you are surest of.
help.timeline.turn: Tap the events from the earliest to the latest, then tap Check.
help.towers.end: You win when the grid is full and every clue matches.
help.towers.goal: Build a tower on every square, with heights from 1 to the grid size and no height repeated in a row or column.
help.towers.tip: A clue of 1 means the tallest tower is right beside it. A clue equal to the grid size means the heights rise in order.
help.towers.turn: Tap a square, then tap a height. Edge numbers show how many towers you can see from that side. Taller towers hide shorter ones.
help.tracks.end: You win when the track runs unbroken from A to B and every count matches.
help.tracks.goal: Complete the train track from A to B. Numbers at the edges count the track squares in each row and column.
help.tracks.tip: The track only goes straight or turns a corner, and it never crosses itself.
help.tracks.turn: Tap an edge between squares to lay track. Press and hold to cross it out. Tap inside a square to mark it as track.
help.tripeaks.end: You win when all three peaks are gone.
help.tripeaks.tip: Long runs without drawing build a streak.
help.tripeaks.turn: Tap a free card that is one higher or one lower than the pile card. King and ace wrap around.
help.truco.end: The first team to the target wins.
help.truco.tip: Bluffing is part of the game; the other side may accept or fold.
help.truco.turn: Play a card each round and win two of three rounds for the hand. You may call truco to raise the stakes, or envido for a side bet.
help.twiddle.end: You win when all the numbers are in order.
help.twiddle.goal: Rotate blocks of tiles until the numbers run in order from the top left.
help.twiddle.tip: Move one tile at a time into place, and leave the last block for the end.
help.twiddle.turn: Tap where tiles meet to turn the block around that point. Press and hold to turn it the other way.
help.undead.end: You win when every square is filled, the totals match, and every edge number is correct.
help.undead.goal: Place a ghost, vampire or zombie in every empty square so every number around the edge is right.
help.undead.tip: Vampires vanish in mirrors. Ghosts show only in mirrors. Zombies show everywhere.
help.undead.turn: Tap a square, then tap a monster. Edge numbers count the monsters you see along that line, including in mirrors.
help.unequal.end: You win when the grid is full and every sign is satisfied.
help.unequal.goal: Fill the grid with digits so none repeats in a row or column, and every sign between squares is true.
help.unequal.tip: In Adjacent mode, a bar means two digits that differ by one. No bar means they do not.
help.unequal.turn: Tap a square, then tap a digit. Press and hold to write small notes instead.
help.unruly.end: You win when every square is colored and all rows and columns follow both rules.
help.unruly.goal: Color every square black or white. Each row and column holds equal numbers of each, and no three in a row match.
help.unruly.tip: Two matching squares in a row force the squares at both ends to be the other color.
help.unruly.turn: Tap a square to color it black. Press and hold to color it white. Tap again to clear it.
help.untangle.end: You win when no lines cross.
help.untangle.goal: Move the points so no line crosses another.
help.untangle.tip: Pull a point with many lines out to the edge first, then arrange the rest around it.
help.untangle.turn: Drag a point to a new spot. Its lines stay attached.
help.ur.end: The first to bear off all seven pieces wins.
help.ur.goal: Bring all seven of your pieces round the board and off first.
help.ur.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter plays, R or Space rolls, H hints, N starts a new game.
help.ur.tip: A piece on the central rosette cannot be captured.
help.ur.turn: Roll the four dice. Move a piece that many squares. Landing on a rosette gives another roll.
help.whereintheworld.end: The round ends after the last place. Closer taps score more.
help.whereintheworld.keys: Arrow keys move the pin. Plus and minus zoom. Enter guesses.
help.whereintheworld.tip: Start from the large shapes and work in.
help.whereintheworld.turn: Read the name, then tap where it is on the map.
help.wikirace.end: You finish at the target. Fewer clicks is better. In Two players, both race the same pair.
help.wikirace.goal: Get from the start article to the target article.
help.wikirace.keys: Press Tab to reach a link, then Enter to follow it.
help.wikirace.tip: Go to a big general article first, then narrow down. Give up is in the Menu.
help.wikirace.turn: Tap links inside the articles. You may not use search.
help.xiangqi.end: You win by checkmate or stalemate. The generals may never face each other with nothing between.
help.xiangqi.keys: Arrow keys move, Enter selects, U undoes, F flips the board, N starts a new game.
help.xiangqi.tip: Keep your general inside the palace.
help.xiangqi.turn: Move one piece. Soldiers move forward, and sideways after they cross the river. Cannons jump over one piece to capture.
help.yacht.end: The game ends when every row is used. The highest total wins.
help.yacht.goal: Score the most over thirteen rows.
help.yacht.tip: A bonus comes if the top six rows reach 63.
help.yacht.turn: Roll five dice up to three times, keeping some between rolls. Then pick a row to score.
help.zimcity.end: Going broke ends the city. Reaching 100,000 people makes it a metropolis, and you can keep building.
help.zimcity.goal: Grow a town into a city people want to live in.
help.zimcity.keys: Arrow keys move the cursor tile, Enter builds there, I inspects it, plus and minus zoom.
help.zimcity.tip: Keep homes away from industry, and raise taxes a step at a time.
help.zimcity.turn: Lay a road, run a power line to it, then zone homes, shops and industry beside it.
hex.swap: Swap rule: the second player may take over the first move
hex.swapAsk: Swap sides and move first, or play as {side}
hex.swapped.blue: Zimi swapped sides. You are blue now. Your turn.
hex.swapped.red: Zimi swapped sides. You are red now. Your turn.
history.2048: 2048 was written by the Italian developer Gabriele Cirulli in 2014 in a weekend. It is a variation on an earlier game called Threes.
history.babel: The Tower of Babel is the story of why people speak many languages. Many words still show that languages share ancestors.
history.backgammon: Backgammon belongs to a family of race games that goes back about 5,000 years. The doubling cube was added in New York in the 1920s.
history.belote: Belote is the national card game of France, and was popular there by the early 1900s. It is related to the Dutch game Klaverjas.
history.bigtwo: Big Two is a climbing game from southern China, popular across East and Southeast Asia. It is played in many places for money and for fun.
history.blackbox: Black Box is a deduction game created by the games designer Eric Solomon in the 1970s. It was first published as a board game, with the balls hidden in a grid. Players fire rays in from the edge and work out what is inside from where each ray comes out.
history.blackjack: Blackjack came from a French and Spanish game called Vingt-et-un. In the 1960s mathematicians showed that counting cards can shift the odds.
history.blast: Grid games with bombs and breakable blocks began on Japanese home computers in 1983. They became a favourite party game for several players at once.
history.bluff: Balderdash was published in 1984, and the older paper game Fictionary is the same idea: invent a definition and fool the others. Here the real definitions come from your Wiktionary.
history.bricks: Bricks follows Breakout, an Atari arcade game of 1976 designed with Steve Wozniak’s help. It was an answer to Pong, played with bricks instead of a net.
history.bridge: Bridge developed from Whist in the late 1800s. Contract Bridge, with bidding as played today, was devised by Harold Vanderbilt on a ship in 1925.
history.bridges: Bridges is a Japanese pencil puzzle called Hashiwokakero, which means build bridges. It appears in puzzle magazines and websites around the world. Every puzzle here can be solved by logic alone.
history.canasta: Canasta was invented in Uruguay in the 1930s. It became a craze in the United States around 1950.
history.carrom: Carrom is a flicking game played across South Asia, popular in India by the 1800s. It is played on a smooth board with four pockets, and the queen is the special coin.
history.checkers: Draughts or checkers has been played in Europe since the Middle Ages. The English rules, with compulsory captures, were written down by the 1700s.
history.chess: Chess comes from a game called chaturanga, played in India by about the 600s. The modern rules, with a powerful queen and bishop, settled in Europe around 1500.
history.chessopenings: Players have named openings for centuries, after people and places: the Ruy Lopez after a 16th-century Spanish priest, the Sicilian after the island. The ECO codes, A00 to E99, come from the Encyclopaedia of Chess Openings, first published in 1974.
history.chesspuzzles: Chess problems were printed in books and newspapers through the 1800s. The puzzles here are different: positions from real games on Lichess, rated by how many players solved them.
history.chinesecheckers: Chinese Checkers was marketed in the United States in the 1930s, and it is neither Chinese nor a checkers game. It comes from a German game called Stern-Halma, which came from the earlier Halma of 1883.
history.circuit: Racing games began in arcades in the 1970s; Atari's Gran Trak 10 of 1974 put a steering wheel and pedals on a cabinet. Top-down racers like this one were the first kind.
history.codebreaker: Code Breaker follows Mastermind, designed by Mordecai Meirowitz and sold from 1972. A similar game on paper, Bulls and Cows, is much older.
history.crazyeights: Crazy Eights is a shedding game related to older games such as Switch and Mau-Mau. It is a family game in many countries, and its commercial cousin Uno appeared in 1971.
history.cribbage: Cribbage was invented in England in the early 1600s by the poet Sir John Suckling. It is still scored on a board with pegs, and sailors long played it at sea.
history.crossing: Getting a small creature across a busy road and a river became an arcade game in 1981, in Japan. The idea is older: the chicken crossing the road is a joke from the 1800s.
history.cube: Cube is based on a Java web game by Paul Scott. The aim is to roll a cube around a grid so that the blue squares end up on its faces. Simon Tatham added grids of triangles, with solids that have more faces.
history.dominoes: Dominoes reached Europe in the 1700s, probably from China, where tile games are much older. The standard set has 28 tiles.
history.dominosa: Dominosa is widely credited to O. S. Adler, whose initials gave the puzzle part of its name. A full set of dominoes is laid out in a rectangle, and then only the numbers are shown. You rebuild the layout from the numbers alone.
history.dotsandboxes: Dots and Boxes was described by the French mathematician Edouard Lucas in 1889. It is played on paper with a pencil, and schoolchildren still play it that way.
history.draughts: International draughts is played on a ten by ten board and was standardised in France in the 1700s. It is very popular in the Netherlands, Russia and West Africa.
history.droppin: GeoGuessr made finding a place on a map a popular game in 2013. Here the map can be your own offline one.
history.durak: Durak is the best known card game in Russia and nearby countries. Its name means fool, and the last player holding cards takes that title.
history.echo: Echo follows Simon, an electronic game made by Ralph Baer and Howard Morrison in 1978. It tests short-term memory with growing sequences of lights.
history.euchre: Euchre came to North America with settlers from Europe and was hugely popular there by the 1800s. Its highest card, the jack of trump, is called the right bower.
history.fifteen: The 15 puzzle appeared in the 1870s and set off a craze in America and Europe in 1880. Mathematicians showed in 1879 that half of all starting positions cannot be solved. Every board here can be.
history.filling: Filling is known in Japan as Fillomino. Each number tells you the size of the region it belongs to. Two regions of the same size may never share an edge.
history.firstlines: Before titles were common, a book was named by its first words, called the incipit. Opening lines are still the part of a book that people remember best.
history.fiveletters: Five-letter word guessing games grew out of an older game called Jotto and of Mastermind. A version posted in 2021 made the format a daily habit for millions of people.
history.flags: National flags in their modern form began in the late 1700s, when the French and American revolutions put flags on the side of the people. Vexillology, the study of flags, got its name in 1957.
history.fleet: Fleet follows a pencil-and-paper game that was played in the early 1900s. A boxed plastic version appeared in the 1960s.
history.flip: Flip belongs to the family of Lights Out puzzles, where a move changes a square and some of its neighbours. Doing a move twice cancels it out, so the order of your moves never matters. That fact lets mathematicians solve these puzzles with algebra.
history.flood: Flood is based on a web game called Flood-It, in which you grow one colour from a corner of the grid. Each move fills every square joined to the corner with a new colour. The move limit in each game comes from a solver written for this collection.
history.fourinarow: Four in a Row is a vertical version of a line-up game. The best known commercial edition appeared in 1974, and the game was solved by computer in 1988.
history.freecell: FreeCell grew out of older patience games with free spaces. Paul Alfille wrote a computer version in the 1970s, and Microsoft put it in Windows from 1991 with numbered deals.
history.galaxies: Galaxies is called Tentaisho in Japan, which means heavenly bodies. It is also known as Spiral Galaxies. Each region must look the same when turned upside down around its dot.
history.gin: Gin Rummy was devised in New York in 1909 by Elwood Baker. It became a craze in the 1930s and 1940s, and was played by many film stars.
history.go: Go was played in China more than 2,000 years ago and spread to Korea and Japan. It has far more possible games than chess, and a computer first beat a top professional in 2016.
history.golf: Golf is a patience game from the 1800s. It is played with one deck and seven columns.
history.gomoku: Gomoku is played on a Go board and has been known in Japan since at least the 1800s. Its name means five points.
history.goproblems: Life-and-death problems are as old as written Go. The Xuanxuan Qijing, compiled in China around 1347, is one of the oldest collections, and Japanese Go houses used problem books to train their players.
history.group: Group is built on the table of a finite group, a layout named for the mathematician Arthur Cayley, who wrote about groups in 1854. Each row and column holds every letter once, like a Latin square, with an extra rule from the group. The collection marks this one as unfinished.
history.hearts: Hearts belongs to a family of trick-taking games from the 1700s where the aim is to avoid points. A computer version came with Windows from 1992.
history.hex: Hex was invented by Piet Hein in Denmark in 1942 and independently by John Nash at Princeton in 1948. It has no draws, and the first player has a proven winning strategy.
history.higherlower: Guessing if the next card or number is higher or lower is an old card game, and a television game show used it from 1978. Here the figures are real, from the lists in your Wikipedia.
history.hnefatafl: Hnefatafl was a Viking Age board game, played across northern Europe. Its rules were lost. What we know comes from a few clues, such as Linnaeus’s account of Sami play in 1732.
history.holdem: Texas Hold’em was played in Texas in the early 1900s and brought to Las Vegas in the 1960s. It became the main game of the World Series of Poker.
history.hopper: Running and jumping across platforms became a genre in the early 1980s, in Japanese arcades and on home consoles. Hopper is our own take on it.
history.inertia: Inertia was written for Windows by Ben Olmstead, who released it so it could join this collection. The ball keeps sliding until a wall or a stop square halts it. That makes the puzzle one of planning ahead.
history.janggi: Janggi is the Korean chess, in its present form since the 1500s. Its pieces are marked with Chinese characters, in two colours.
history.jigsaw: The first jigsaw puzzles were maps cut up by a London mapmaker in the 1760s, to teach geography. The name comes from the saws used to cut them.
history.kart: Kart racing games, with items to grab and drifting to master, took off on home consoles in Japan in 1992. Real go-karts are older: the first was built in California in 1956.
history.keen: Keen is this collection's version of KenKen. The Japanese teacher Tetsuya Miyamoto invented KenKen in 2004 to help his students practise arithmetic and logic. Each cage gives a number and the sign to reach it.
history.koikoi: Koi-Koi is played with hanafuda, Japanese flower cards, which date from the 1600s. Nintendo began as a maker of hanafuda cards in 1889.
history.lander: Lander follows Lunar Lander, a game that first ran on computers in 1969, the year of the Moon landing. Its arcade version of 1979 used vector graphics.
history.lastline: Last Line follows Space Invaders, a Japanese arcade game of 1978. A common story says it was so popular that it caused a shortage of coins.
history.letterbyletter: Guessing a word letter by letter is an old pencil-and-paper game, often called Hangman, played by the 1800s. This one keeps a balloon up instead.
history.liarsdice: Liar’s Dice is a bluffing game with many names, played in pubs and on ships for centuries. A form of it appears in a well-known pirate film.
history.lightup: Light Up is called Akari in Japan, which means light. You place lamps so that every square is lit and no lamp shines on another. Numbers on black squares say how many lamps touch them.
history.loopy: Loopy belongs to the Slitherlink family, a Japanese loop puzzle published by Nikoli. Here it is played on many kinds of grid, from squares and triangles to hexagons and Penrose tilings.
history.ludo: Ludo comes from Pachisi, a race game played in India by the 1500s. It was patented in England as Ludo in 1896.
history.magnets: Magnets is credited to the puzzle site Janko, and James Harvey added it to this collection. Each domino is either a magnet with a plus and a minus end, or blank. Like poles may never touch.
history.mahjong: Mahjong tiles came together in China in the 1800s. This solo matching game, with tiles stacked in layouts, is a different game, made popular by computers from the 1980s.
history.mahjong4: Mahjong is a four-player game that took its modern form in China in the 1800s. The Hong Kong style played here is the classic one before newer scoring rules.
history.makruk: Makruk is the Thai chess, and may be older than the western game. Its queen is a weak piece, which keeps games slow and careful.
history.mancala: Mancala is the name of a family of sowing games played across Africa and Asia for many centuries. Oware comes from West Africa and Kalah is the form played most in the United States.
history.map: The four colour theorem says that any map can be coloured with four colours so that no neighbours match. It was first posed in 1852 and proved in 1976 with the help of a computer. This puzzle gives you a partly coloured map to finish.
history.memory: Memory, also called Concentration or Pairs, is a card-matching game known since the 1800s or earlier. Children often beat adults at it.
history.minesweeper: Minesweeper grew from 1960s and 1970s computer games. Microsoft included it in Windows from 1990, and it was meant to teach mouse skills.
history.minicrossword: The first newspaper crossword was made by Arthur Wynne for the New York World in 1913. Small grids like this one became a daily habit when newspapers put them online.
history.morris: Nine Men’s Morris was played in the Roman world and across medieval Europe. Boards for it are cut into the stones of old buildings, such as some cathedral cloisters.
history.mosaic: Mosaic goes by many names, including Fill-a-Pix, Nurie-Puzzle and Count and Darken. Didi Kohen contributed it to this collection. Each clue counts the black squares in the block of nine around it, itself included.
history.muncher: Maze games where you eat dots while being chased became a craze in 1980, when a Japanese arcade game made them famous around the world. Its four chasers each had their own way of hunting you.
history.net: Net comes from a family of network games that includes NetWalk, from 1996. Simon Tatham first saw it as the Flash game FreeNet, by Pavils Jurjans. You turn the tiles so that every wire joins the center with no loops.
history.netslide: Netslide joins the networks of Net to the sliding rows and columns of Sixteen. Richard Boulton contributed it to this collection. You shift whole lines of tiles instead of turning single tiles.
history.noughts: Tic-Tac-Toe, called noughts and crosses in Britain, is played all over the world and was known in ancient Rome in a similar form. With perfect play, it always ends in a draw.
history.paddles: Paddles follows Pong, made by Atari in 1972. It was one of the first video games to be a commercial success.
history.palisade: Palisade is based on Five Cells, a puzzle from the Japanese publisher Nikoli. Jonas Kölker contributed it to this collection. Every region has the same size, and each number counts the borders around its square.
history.pattern: Pattern is a nonogram, a picture puzzle also known as Picross or Griddlers. Japanese puzzle designers invented nonograms in the late 1980s. They spread through magazines and video games.
history.pearl: Pearl is Masyu, a Japanese loop puzzle published by Nikoli. The loop must turn at every black pearl and run straight through every white one. Here it can also be drawn in the style of Loopy.
history.pegs: Pegs is peg solitaire, a game for one player known at the court of Louis XIV of France in the late 1600s. Pegs jump over each other and are removed, until one is left. The boards here are cross-shaped, octagonal or random.
history.pet: Virtual pets that need daily care became a worldwide craze in 1996, starting in Japan. This one grows up over real days.
history.pinball: Pinball came from tabletop bagatelle games of the 1700s. Flippers were added in 1947, which turned it from a game of chance into a game of skill.
history.pyramid: Pyramid is an old patience game that was already described in books in the 1800s. Pairs add up to 13, so the king counts alone.
history.quest: Adventure games began with Adventure on a mainframe in the 1970s and moved to home consoles in 1979. Top-down action adventures grew from them.
history.quizzical: Quiz games grew with radio and television in the 1900s. These questions are made fresh from the articles and words in your own library.
history.range: Range is Kuromasu, a Japanese puzzle whose name means black squares. Each number counts the white squares you can see from it in straight lines. The white squares must stay joined in one area.
history.rect: Rectangles is Shikaku, a Japanese puzzle whose name means square shape. Nikoli helped make it popular. You divide the grid into rectangles, each holding one number that equals its area.
history.reversi: Reversi was published in England in 1883. The version called Othello, with a fixed start, was patented in Japan in 1971.
history.roadrush: In the 1980s, arcade racers drew a road that seemed to rush toward you by scaling flat strips of it, long before true 3D. This game draws its road the same way.
history.rocks: Rocks follows Asteroids, an Atari arcade game of 1979. In both games, a rock you shoot splits into smaller ones.
history.samegame: Same Game was written in 1985 by Kuniaki Moribe under the name Chain Shot. It was later ported to many computers and renamed SameGame. Bigger groups score far more than small ones.
history.scopa: Scopa is an Italian card game known since at least the 1700s. It is played with a 40-card Italian deck, and a scopa is a sweep of the table.
history.shogi: Shogi is the Japanese chess, in its present form by the 1500s. It is the only major chess game where captured pieces can be dropped back on the board for you.
history.signpost: Signpost is credited to the puzzle site Janko, which calls it Pfeilpfad, German for arrow path. James Harvey added it to this collection. You number the squares into one chain, each arrow pointing along the line to the next.
history.singles: Singles is Hitori, which means alone in Japanese. You shade squares until no number repeats in any row or column. The shaded squares may not touch, and the white ones must stay joined.
history.sixteen: Sixteen is a relative of the 15 puzzle, which caused a craze in America and Europe in 1880. There is no gap here. Whole rows and columns slide and wrap around instead.
history.skat: Skat was invented in Altenburg, Germany, in the early 1800s. It is the national card game of Germany, and has its own official court of rules.
history.skydetective: Stargazers have named the bright stars and planets for thousands of years. This game works out the real sky from the date, the time and where you are.
history.slant: Slant is a Japanese pencil puzzle called Gokigen Naname. You fill every square with a diagonal line and may never close a loop. Numbers tell how many lines touch each point.
history.snake: Snake dates back to arcade games of the 1970s. It reached millions of people in 1998, when it came on Nokia phones.
history.snakesandladders: Snakes and Ladders came from India, where it was a teaching game about good and bad deeds. It reached England in the 1800s.
history.sokoban: Hiroyuki Imabayashi made Sokoban, Japanese for warehouse keeper, and Thinking Rabbit published it in Japan in 1982. The levels here come from Boxoban, a set DeepMind generated and published in 2018.
history.solitaire: Patience games for one player were played in Europe by the late 1700s. The Klondike version became the best known after Windows 3.0 included it in 1990, partly to teach people to use a mouse.
history.spades: Spades was invented in the United States in the 1930s and grew out of Whist. It became very popular in the 1940s, and bidding Nil is its most famous move.
history.spellingbee: Spelling bees began in the United States in the 1800s as a school contest, and the national one has run since 1925. This game borrows the name for a word puzzle with seven letters.
history.spider: Spider is a patience game with two decks, known in print by the early 1900s. It reached most players as part of Windows from 2001.
history.stacker: This falling-block game follows Tetris, written by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow in 1984. Its pieces are made from four squares, called tetrominoes.
history.sudoku: Number puzzles with these rules appeared in a US magazine in 1979 as Number Place. A Japanese publisher named it Sudoku in the 1980s, and it became a craze in the 2000s.
history.teenpatti: Teen Patti is a three-card poker game from India. It is often played at festivals such as Diwali.
history.telephone: Telephone, called Chinese whispers in Britain, is a party game where a message is passed along and changes on the way. Here the message is a clue.
history.tents: Tents is a pencil puzzle found on many websites. Each tent must sit next to a tree of its own, and no two tents may touch, even at a corner. The numbers at the edges count the tents in each row and column.
history.tienlen: Tien Len is Vietnam’s favourite card game, and its name means forward. It is closely related to other climbing games, like Big Two.
history.timeline: Timelines were drawn by Joseph Priestley in 1765, when he put the lives of famous people on a chart. Ordering events by when they happened is still the quickest way to see how history fits together.
history.towers: Towers is also known as Skyscrapers. Each clue counts how many towers you can see when you look along a line, because tall towers hide short ones. Harder puzzles give some heights in advance.
history.tracks: Tracks was contributed to this collection by James Harvey. The rails are straight or turn a quarter turn, and the line may never cross itself. The numbers at the edges count the track squares in each row and column.
history.tripeaks: TriPeaks is a patience game in the Golf family. It spread widely on computers from the 1990s.
history.truco: Truco is a trick-taking game played in Argentina, Uruguay, Brazil and Spain. Bluffing and calling the stakes up are central to it.
history.twiddle: Simon Tatham first met this kind of puzzle in the GameCube game Metroid Prime 2, where a door puzzle in the Main Gyro Chamber is a special case. He generalised it into Twiddle. You rotate groups of tiles to put the numbers in order.
history.undead: Undead was invented by David Millar under the name Haunted Mirror Maze. Steffen Bauer contributed it to this collection. Vampires vanish in mirrors, ghosts show only in mirrors, and zombies show everywhere.
history.unequal: Unequal is Futoshiki, from the Japanese word for inequality. It was invented by Tamaki Seto in 2001. This version also has an Adjacent mode, where a bar marks two digits that differ by exactly one.
history.unruly: Unruly is also called Binairo or Takuzu. Each row and column must hold equal numbers of the two colours. No three squares in a row may match.
history.untangle: Untangle follows Planarity, a game made by John Tantalo in 2005. A graph is planar when it can be drawn without crossing lines. Every puzzle here is made from a drawing that has none.
history.ur: The Royal Game of Ur takes its name from boards found in the royal tombs of Ur, in modern Iraq, dated to about 2600 BC. A clay tablet from 177 BC helped scholars work out the rules.
history.whereintheworld: Learning places from a map is one of the oldest ways to study geography. Here your own library supplies the places.
history.wikirace: Wiki Race is a game people made up on Wikipedia, going from one article to another by links alone. It works because the links form a web.
history.xiangqi: Xiangqi is the Chinese chess, played for roughly a thousand years in forms like today’s. The board has a river across the middle and a palace for each general.
history.yacht: Yacht is a dice game that was sold in the United States in the early 1900s. It is the ancestor of Yahtzee, which was trademarked in 1956.
history.zimcity: Will Wright's city simulator came out in 1989. Its code was released as Micropolis in 2008, and Graeme McCutcheon ported it to JavaScript. ZimCity runs that port.
